doc.title: Paquito D'Rivera — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Cachao, Chocolate and his father's musician friends
summary: The musicians met at a standing-room bar near his father's office; as a child he inherited their friendship and wanted to be as elegant as Chocolate Armenteros.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: And these musicians, like Cachao and Chico O’ Farrill and Chocolate Armenteros, and other musicians who were associates and friends of your father’s, did they come around the house?

Not so much; they get together in, there was a very nice, I don’t know how the word—a bar, a salon, a deli—the standing up; there was no sitting area, so the musicians used to go and talk about baseball and music and all of that. And, my father had that office two blocks away from that place. So, I don’t remember seeing the musicians too much around my house, but around Los Palados bar, or cafeteria.
As child, did he ever take you around these musicians?

Oh, all the time; all the time. Many people think that I am older just because I inherited those friends. I inherited the friendship of Cachao and Chocolate and Chico O’ Farrill and all those guys. Those were my friends. Well, I made friends later on, but still today, some of those old guys are my friends. Those are the ones who come to my house to have black beans and rice together.
As a young child, when you’d be around these musicians, what did that mean for you? Did that encourage you to want to be a musician as well, or what?

I think, from the very beginning I have no choice. I was meant to be a musician. No surrounding of those people; in those days I didn’t know that it was so great, that it was going to make history. They were just the friends of my father and the musicians who played in the clubs and the symphony and all those places. But they make my mind up for me, that I wanted to be like them. For example, I love to imitate Chocolate’s way of dressing; he was, Chocolate was the most elegant musician in Havana. He always had his cut, uh suits and the very, very skinny ties, and the elegant shoes. I wanted to be like Chocolate, and still today, I want to be like Chocolate. [Both laugh] But nobody can be like Chocolate; he’s unique.
